name: Company lesson template
purpose: One fixed format for explaining any company to a first-time investor. Every company lesson, written by a person or drafted by a model, follows it. The checker (scripts/check-lessons.cjs) and any future drafting step read this file, so there is one definition of the format.
reader: Someone starting to invest who has never met this industry. After the opening they should be able to say what the company does, who pays it and for what, what costs money, and what could make the business harder.

sections.answers: What does the company actually do?
sections.write: One or two plain sentences naming the real products, work or service. Say what people, machines or software do. An industry label alone is not an explanation.

sections.answers: What is the actual work, in everyday words?
sections.write: Describe the object or task before its technical name. Use verbs such as unload, store, move, build, connect, test, lend, collect and repair.

sections.answers: How does it earn money, and what does it spend money on?
sections.write: Separate service fees, sale of goods, subscriptions and interest. Name the main costs. State that the customer's whole payment is not profit.

sections.answers: Who pays, and what does the payment buy?
sections.write: Name the customer type, who actually pays and what they get. If the user of the product is not the payer, say so.

sections.answers: What mainly decides whether the business does well?
sections.write: Two or three concrete things, such as prices, volumes, costs or contract terms. No numbers.

sections.answers: What are the main products or services, grouped sensibly?
sections.write: Each item names a group, gives recognisable examples as one sentence, then explains in plain words what that group is and why a customer buys it.

sections.answers: Which words or ideas must I know before the rest makes sense?
sections.write: Define each essential term or abbreviation where the reader first needs it. Phrase the title as a question.

sections.answers: What happens from the work or delivery to the bill and the customer's payment?
sections.write: A short sequence in time order. Show that revenue, profit and cash received are different things.

sections.answers: What is distinctive about this company's economics?
sections.write: Concrete reasons this business can earn more or less than a similar one. Explain mechanisms and avoid claims about quality.
Five research questions. Each has the question, a plain reason it matters and what evidence to compare. These are questions to investigate, not findings.

sections.answers: What could make the business harder?
sections.write: Plain risks tied to how this company earns and spends. Repeat only what a source says. Never imply wrongdoing unless a filing says so.

sections.answers: What recent development should I know about?
sections.write: One dated, sourced development. Keep plans described as plans.

sections.answers: Did I understand the main idea?
sections.write: One self-check question and its answer, about the business mechanics and not about numbers.
Primary company or exchange disclosures first. Every link must be https.

sections.answers: How should I read this company's reported numbers?
sections.write: The only place in the lesson where actual amounts may appear. Keep period, units, scope and the profit definition together. Never allocate company profit to a brand or product.

sections.answers: When was this read against its sources?
sections.write: Day, month name and year, for example 31 October 2026.

optional.write: A worked example with made-up numbers that shows how the business turns work into a bill, cost and profit. Every item must say in its own words that it is fictional or illustrative. Never use a real customer, contract, price, fee or revenue source. This is the only section besides financialNotes where amounts may appear.
Use when current exchange listing is unverified.
Names of offering cards that are discontinued or sold.
Replaces the product list in the company file.
Source label for the product list.
A verified financial record. Only added by a separate financial review.

rules.abbreviationsNeedingDefinition: Capitalised abbreviations of 2 to 6 letters must be explained where they first appear, unless they are on the allowed list.
